newsitem.title: USA: Clinton names team to push for campaign reform.
newsitem.headline: Clinton names team to push for campaign reform.

text.p: President Bill Clinton named a high-profile team to promote campaign finance reform on Monday in a move dismissed by a Republican leader as a mere diversion from the fund-raising woes dogging Clinton.

The Democratic president selected former Democratic Vice President Walter Mondale, until recently his ambassador to Japan, and former Kansas Republican Sen. Nancy Kassebaum Baker to lead a "crusade" to educate the public on campaign reforms.

The announcement was made at a White House ceremony by Vice President Al Gore, who stood in for Clinton following his knee surgery and said that although the president "is having a little trouble walking today, he is committed to taking all the strides we need to reform our campaign finance system."

Clinton has set a goal of July 4 for passage of a campaign finance reform bill proposed by a bipartisan group in the Senate and House of Representatives. It would limit donations and spending and end vast flows of cash given directly to the parties -- called "soft money" because, unlike money given candidates, it is unlimited and unregulated.
"Today we push our crusade still further," Gore said in announcing the appointment of Mondale and Kassebaum to push the legislative reform proposal with the American public.
"If we don't act quickly, and if we don't act in a truly bipartisan fashion, reform will fail this year as it has year in and year out," he said.
Senate Republican leader Trent Lott, whose cooperation is essential to pass such a bill in the Republican-majority Congress, gave Clinton's new initiative the back of his hand.
"I assume it's just another effort to distract attention from all the problems that they're having to deal with," Lott told reporters at his daily news conference.

Clinton and his party are the focus of alleged campaign finance irregularities being investigated by a Justice Department task force and by Senate and House committees. The main questions are whether he exchanged White House access for campaign cash or even allowed foreign donors to influence U.S. policy decisions.
Gore is also involved, having admitted making telephone calls from his office to solicit donations. But he denies any wrongdoing in that effort, as does the president.
The Democratic party has returned some $3 million in illegal or questionable donations, with 75 percent of them raised from sources in Asia or with Asian business ties.

Although congressional hearings are still in the preparatory phase, House Judiciary Committee Chairman Henry Hyde, an Illinois Republican, said on Sunday his committee is studying how to go about impeachment proceedings in event a "smoking gun" is found involving Clinton or Gore.

Hyde commented in a television interview on a request from Representative Bob Barr, a Georgia Republican, to have the committee consider whether the fund-raising allegations would justify an impeachment investigation.

"We are studying the laws of impeachment, the procedures of impeachment," Hyde said. "I would like to have some evidence -- I would like to have at least one smoking gun -- before we proceed with impeachment."
The U.S. Constitution warrants impeachment by the House and removal from office after Senate trial as a remedy for "high crimes and misdemeanors."
Few if any of Clinton's critics assert he has committed such crimes.

The last impeachment proceedings occurred in 1974 when the House Judiciary Committee approved three articles of impeachment -- for abuse of power, obstruction of justice and contempt of Congress -- against President Richard Nixon in the Watergate scandal.
That scandal led to the last reforms of campaign finance abuses. But experts agree that those regulations are full of loopholes, and campaign spending has grown steadily bigger.
